newsitem.title: UK: UK jobless figure vindicates Tory policy - Heseltine.
newsitem.headline: UK jobless figure vindicates Tory policy - Heseltine.

text.p: Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine said on Wednesday the economic policy of Britain's Conservative government had been vindicated by another fall in unemployment.

Citing figures released on Wednesday which showed a 68,200 drop in unemployment in February from January, Heseltine told Reuters that inflation worries and repeated calls for a rise in interest rates had proved unfounded.
"The man who has been proved right is the Chancellor of the Exchequer - the inflation figures have been very competitive and are the best test of whether the chancellor has got it right."

Britain's unemployment rate fell to a six-year low of 6.2 percent in February, providing a welcome boost for the embattled Conservative government, seen as lagging far behind the Labour opposition ahead of the May 1 polls.

Heseltine said the important factor about the latest rise in earnings -- five percent in January -- was whether it was being funded by productivity, said Heseltine. "The benign circumstance we want to see is where people's living standards are rising but they're being paid for by improved performance. So far that's been the case." He said Chancellor Kenneth Clarke would monitor the position and take whatever action was appropriate. "But he doesn't think that any action is necessary at the moment," said Heseltine. Heseltine was speaking at the official opening of telephone- based direct motor insurer Hastings Direct new British headquarters. Hastings, backed by Japanese insurance giant Chiyoda Fire & Marine has been trading since January and was an important example of investment flowing into Britain from overseas, said Heseltine. He defended the government's wait-and-see policy on the single European currency which has been criticised by some companies as likely to deter future investment in Britain. "People making decisions about investing in Britain or Europe will want to know about our position on the single European currency but they would not be sympathetic to its introduction on terms that would make no economic sense."

"They would respect Britain's position as a leading European nation taking part in negotiations and preserving its options until the facts are clear." Doubts were being raised all over Europe about the possibility of economic convergence taking place on the original timescale "no more so than in Germany itself", he said.
